source: Hepler & Feltz (2012) Take the first heuristic, self-efficacy, and decision-making in sport
finding: In a video basketball task, people used take-the-first (TTF) on most trials, earlier options were better than later ones, and the final option was usually meaningfully chosen. Number of options did not change decision confidence.
numbers: N=72 students; 13 trials in each of two video tasks; TTF used on 70% of trials; higher self-efficacy went with more TTF and fewer options.
quote: earlier generated options were better than later ones, first options were meaningfully generated, and final options were meaningfully selected
limits: Abstract read via PubMed; the full paper was not obtained, so no effect sizes. Students, not elite players. Verbal option generation.
agent_relevance: A first option from a well-practised source is usually the best one, but this is shown for people with domain practice. For an LLM, check that the first attempt really comes from a strong prior.

source: Musculus, Ruggeri, Raab & Lobinger (2019) A developmental perspective on option generation and selection
finding: Children generated few options, in decreasing order of quality, and picked the first one. Older children picked the first option more often and faster. Time limits led to fewer and better options.
numbers: N=73 children aged 6-13; four measurement waves; soccer task.
limits: Abstract only; no per-wave numbers. Same research network as the original TTF work.
agent_relevance: TTF use grows with practice and time pressure. A time or token limit may push toward the first option, which is only good if the first option is good.

source: Haeusser et al. (2014) The effects of caffeine on option generation and subsequent choice
finding: In everyday scenarios, people tended to choose the first option they generated. Caffeine reduced the number of options and the time to the first option but did not change the tendency to take the first. Familiarity of the scenario did not change it either.
numbers: N=47, double-blind, 300 mg caffeine vs placebo; high and low familiarity scenarios.
limits: Abstract only. Taking the first held even in low-familiarity scenarios, which goes against the claim that it needs expertise; it may be a default habit.
agent_relevance: Taking the first option is a default habit, not proof of skill. The scaffold needs a check that does not depend on familiarity.

source: Laborde & Raab (2013) The tale of hearts and reason: the influence of mood on decision making
finding: Two studies with handball videos replicated earlier TTF results across expertise levels and moods.
numbers: Study 1: 30 nonexperts, 30 near-experts, 30 experts (between subjects); Study 2: 30 nonexperts (within subjects); 31 3D handball videos.
limits: Abstract only. Same lab group (Raab) as the original, so not independent.
agent_relevance: TTF is repeatable within one lab and one sport. No independent lab replication was found.

source: Chen, Ang, Cusin, Fava & Pizzagalli (2025) Task design and heuristics in a knowledge-free option generation task
finding: In a task with no domain knowledge, options did not follow the take-the-first pattern: later paths were less unique, and more options went with lower average uniqueness (less-is-more), not higher quality.
numbers: N=44 healthy people and 54 with major depression; 1.5 minute path generation task; normalized uniqueness fell with option index, which TTF does not predict.
quote: normalized path uniqueness decreased with the path index, contrary to the results predicted by the TTF heuristic
limits: Abstract only. Not a sport or expert sample, so it is a boundary case, not a refutation of expert TTF. Secondary analysis of existing data.
agent_relevance: Quality-ordered options need knowledge. When there is nothing to recognise, the first option has no special status; the scaffold should not trust a first draft on novel tasks.

source: Hepler & Kovacs (2017) Influence of acute stress on decision outcomes and heuristics
finding: Mental or physical stress did not change TTF frequency, number of options, first-option quality or final decision quality. Mental stress slowed the first option and the final decision.
numbers: N=68; 8 video basketball trials per condition (no stress, mental stress, physical stress at 13 RPE).
limits: Abstract only. Same first author as d01, so not independent.
agent_relevance: Quality of a first answer held under load while speed fell; supports a fast-first mode being robust to pressure.

source: Raab & Laborde (2011) When to blink and when to think
finding: Handball players who preferred intuition made faster and better choices than deliberative players; experts were more intuitive than near-experts and nonexperts.
numbers: N=54 handball players of different expertise levels.
limits: Abstract only. Preference measured by questionnaire; correlational.
agent_relevance: Supports expert use of a fast first choice, but via a trait, not a mode that switches with the task.

source: Ramanayaka, Dickson & Rayne (2024) Heuristics in sport: a scoping review
finding: Of 38 included studies, 16 tested fast and frugal heuristics, and 8 of those tested take-the-first. Most studies are on football and basketball.
numbers: 2019 records screened; 38 included; TTF n=8, recognition heuristic n=7, gut instinct n=1.
limits: Abstract only. A scoping review, so no pooled effect size and no quality weighting. The count shows TTF evidence is thin.
agent_relevance: Answers Gap 1: the take-the-first literature is eight sport studies, no meta-analysis, and no failed replication in an expert sample was found (one non-expert boundary case, d05).

source: Soccer referees' yellow card decision-making: analytical vs intuitive style, experts vs novices (2024) Front Psychol 15:1415170
finding: Experts did equally well with intuitive and analytical style. Novices did better when made to reason analytically. This is a measured boundary: intuition pays only with experience.
numbers: N=60 (30 experts, 30 novices). Main effect of style F(1,58)=5.291, p=.025, partial eta2=.084 (analytic .763 vs intuitive .747). Expert accuracy .843 vs novice .666 (F=326.4). Style x level F(1,58)=20.09. Experts: analytic .835 vs intuitive .851 (n.s.). Novices: analytic .690 vs intuitive .643 (p<.05).
limits: Referees, video fouls, one country. Experts were also more overconfident under intuitive style. The paper reports eta2=0.000 for the interaction, which is a typo; the F value is used here.
agent_relevance: Closes Gap 2 in part: this is the best measured novice vs expert split found. Recognition is safe when the system has the knowledge; an agent with weak prior knowledge of a domain should be sent to deliberate.

source: Elgebli, Hall & Phipps (2025) Community pharmacists' decision-making patterns in clinical prescription checking: a simulation-based study
finding: Pharmacists mostly used pattern recognition but moved to a more analytical approach when they met an atypical prescription, as RPD says. Actions after recognition varied and were hesitant.
numbers: N=12 pharmacists in England; three simulated prescriptions; concurrent think-aloud; deductive coding using Klein's RPD model.
limits: Small, qualitative, coded with RPD's own scheme, so it cannot count as an independent test of RPD. No percentages in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Shows the mode switch on atypicality in a non-fire domain, but qualitatively. Atypicality was the trigger, which fits a coverage check.

source: Mansoori et al. (2025) Cognitive task analysis of resident physicians' fluid decisions in septic shock (ATS Scholar 6:448)
finding: Residents (novices) used rules of thumb and showed premature closure, confirmation bias and status quo bias. A fixed volume rule (stop above 3-5 L) was applied even when evidence said otherwise.
numbers: 11 of 23 eligible third-year residents interviewed (median 7 days after the case, IQR 6.5-11); 71 cues identified; rater agreement Fleiss kappa=0.64; critical decision method coded with the RPD template.
limits: 11 interviewees, recall after days, RPD template coding. Not a count of recognition share. Novices, so it shows what recognition looks like without sound patterns.
agent_relevance: Shows what a recognition mode looks like when the stored patterns are weak: it closes early and keeps the default. A scaffold needs a counter-check that is not self-generated.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026), as read in PMC13100097: their description of Calderwood, Klein & Crandall (1988)
finding: Secondary account only: Calderwood et al. compared three class B players with three masters in blitz and slower games (40 moves in 90 min). The weaker players did worse in blitz; the masters seemed immune. The review criticises the tiny sample. The original paper and Klein et al. (1995) were not obtained (publisher pages returned 403, abstracts null in Semantic Scholar).
numbers: 3 class B players vs 3 masters, blitz vs 40 moves in 90 min.
limits: Second-hand and N=6. Contradicted by Vidulich and Tsang's own large-sample result (even top experts blundered more in blitz). No option counts from Klein et al. (1995) were found anywhere.
agent_relevance: Do not cite the 1988 result as showing recognition is time-immune. Gap 7 stays open for exact numbers.

source: Schultz et al. (2025) Mastering Board Games by External and Internal Planning with Language Models (arXiv 2412.12119)
finding: The two search gains refer to different search sizes. +68 internal Elo is at 100 MCTS simulations. The conclusion's 'approximately +300' matches only 500 to 2000 simulations in Table 1. Gains rise roughly with the log of simulations.
numbers: Text: 'MAV-MCTS with just 100 simulations achieves an internal Elo 68 higher than the searchless MAV'. Table 1 chess, columns internal/external, rows paired by order (inferred): MAV 1367/2923; 100 sims 1435/2988; 500 sims 1655/3170; 1000 sims 1689/3191; 2000 sims about 1707/3209. Conclusion: '+300 Elo points even with a fairly limited search budget'.
quote: MAV-MCTS with just 100 simulations achieves an internal Elo 68 higher than the searchless MAV
limits: Table text was garbled by PDF extraction, so row to column pairing is inferred from ordering and should be checked against the PDF figure. External Elo is anchored to Stockfish blitz, so the paper itself says MCTS agents' external Elo is not accurate.
agent_relevance: Cite +68 at 100 simulations and about +300 at 500-2000, never '+300 with limited search' alone. Search gains cost real simulations; a recognition-only mode forgoes them.

source: Monroe & Chalmers (2024) Mastering Chess with a Transformer Model (arXiv 2409.12272) compared with Ruoss et al. (2024)
finding: The 93.5% puzzle score for the Ruoss 270M model is Monroe and Chalmers' own re-evaluation, not Ruoss's number. Ruoss reports 95.4%. Monroe says it follows the Ruoss method on the Ruoss puzzle database but plots puzzles rated 1000-3000, so the subset likely differs.
numbers: Monroe Table II: GC-270M Elo 2299, puzzles 93.5; GC-136M 92.1; GC-9M 85.5; AlphaZero-policy 61.0; their CF-240M-policy 93.5 at 12.8B FLOPS. Ruoss Table 1: 270M 95.4, 136M 94.5, 9M 88.9, AlphaZero policy 56.1; Ruoss puzzles rated 399-2867, 10K set.
limits: Neither paper states the cause. The pattern (Ruoss models 2-3 points lower in Monroe, AlphaZero policy 5 points higher) is not uniform, so the subset explanation is plausible but unproven.
agent_relevance: Keep the two numbers apart. Report 95.4% for the Ruoss paper and 93.5% only when quoting Monroe's re-run.

source: Wen et al. (2024) DiLu: A knowledge-driven approach to autonomous driving with LLMs (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2309.16292)
finding: A memory of 40 text experiences gives 70% success in the setting where it was collected, but 35% in a harder setting (more lanes, denser traffic). The RL baseline dropped by 85% there. So accuracy does fall away from the stored cases, though less than for RL.
numbers: lane-4-density-2: DiLu 70% (40 memory items) vs RL (GRAD) 69% after 600,000 training episodes; lane-5-density-3: DiLu 35%, GRAD 85% relative drop; 10 test scenarios per setting. No memory (0-shot): median success steps below 5 of 30. 3-shot with 20 items: median 13 steps in the home setting falling to 5 in the harder one; 5-shot fell less.
limits: Only three settings, 10 seeds each, one simulator (highway-env). No fine-grained distance measure. 'Matches RL' rests on 10 scenarios.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: one step of distance halves success. No decay curve exists. An agent needs an explicit coverage check.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu & Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters (arXiv 2408.03314)
finding: The best use of extra tokens depends on question difficulty. On easy questions (levels 1-2) more beam search lowers accuracy and sequential revision is best. On harder questions (levels 3-4) beam search beats best-of-N. On the hardest (level 5) nothing helps much. Adaptive allocation matches best-of-N with up to 4x less compute.
numbers: MATH split into five difficulty bins; budgets 4, 16, 64, 256 generations; compute-optimal strategy uses up to 4x less test-time compute than best-of-N; in a FLOPs-matched test, test-time compute beat a 14x larger model only where the small model had non-trivial success.
limits: MATH with a trained process reward model, not an RPD-framed fast path plus code check. Bins are by model pass rate. This is the closest measured break-even by difficulty found; it does not test 'one attempt plus code check'.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: easy items want cheap sequential checking; extra search pays on medium-hard items. The pass rate of a few quick samples can serve as the difficulty signal.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2306.09896)
finding: At equal sample budget, 'generate, test, then repair' is often no better than just sampling more. Gains are modest, differ by subset, and are sometimes absent. They are larger on harder problems, and large when the feedback comes from a stronger model or a human.
numbers: HumanEval and APPS; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Code Llama. GPT-4 on APPS beat the baseline by up to 8%; GPT-3.5 up to 34% relative gain on competition-level problems. 2 samples plus 10 repairs each (22 total) scored 0.97x pass@22; one config scored 1.05x pass@20. Human feedback raised repair success 1.58x (33.3% to 52.6%).
limits: Unit-test-based feedback in code, not open reasoning. The paper counts cost at equal budget, which is what the gap asks. No RPD framing.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: a fast first attempt plus a repair check does not reliably beat plain resampling at equal budget. A check helps most when the model's own feedback is not the bottleneck.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs (arXiv 2412.21187)
finding: Long-reasoning models spend far more tokens on trivial questions, and the first solution is nearly always already correct. Trimming later solutions cut tokens with no accuracy loss.
numbers: '2 plus 3': 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one example produced 13 solutions. In more than 92% of cases the first solution round was correct; the first round was under 60% of tokens; self-training cut MATH500 tokens by 48.6% (QwQ-32B-Preview) with accuracy kept.
limits: Models QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1; math sets ASDIV, MATH500, GSM8K, GPQA, AIME. The 92% figure is for the sets analysed in Figure 5, which include easy sets.
agent_relevance: Direct support that on easy items a recognition-style first pass is enough and extra deliberation is wasted tokens.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.01798)
finding: Asking a model to re-check its own answer without outside feedback does not help and often hurts, because the model changes right answers to wrong ones. GPT-3.5 kept its first answer in 74.7% of GSM8K cases.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 (standard, rounds 1, 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49 to 49 to 43. With oracle labels GPT-4 reached 97.5 on GSM8K.
limits: Table values read from garbled PDF text; row order inferred. Intrinsic self-check is not the same as RPD's mental simulation, but it is the closest tested analog.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 4: a 'does my first answer hold up' prompt carries no information unless it uses an external check. First-answer survival is not a useful switch signal by itself.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang & Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency (arXiv 2305.11860)
finding: Stopping sampling when the answers drawn so far agree strongly (a Dirichlet model of vote shares) cuts samples a lot with almost no accuracy loss.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, 3 LLMs: up to 7.9x fewer samples, average 3.3x fewer (abstract; conclusion says 2 to 4 times), average accuracy drop below 0.1%.
limits: Agreement and margin between the top answers are the signal tested, compared to full majority voting at fixed budget. Gains are on tasks where self-consistency works.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a tested switch signal. Agreement of a few short attempts is a cheap, validated signal to stop early, i.e. to stay in recognition mode.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency for Multi-step Reasoning (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2401.10480)
finding: Sample in windows and stop when a whole window gives one answer. Large cut in samples at similar accuracy.
numbers: Average sampling reduced by: MATH 33.8%, GSM8K 80.1%, StrategyQA 76.8%, CommonsenseQA 78.5%, Coin Flip 84.2%, Last Letters 67.4%; window size 5 (8 for MATH).
limits: Savings are smallest on the hardest set (MATH). Needs windows of 5 or 8 samples.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: window unanimity is a tested stop rule; smaller savings on hard items is itself a difficulty signal.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (arXiv 2502.06233)
finding: Weighting sampled answers by the model's own confidence finds the right answer with fewer samples than plain majority vote.
numbers: 9 models and 4 datasets: required reasoning paths reduced by over 40% on average; also introduces a within-question confidence test.
limits: Confidence is the same model's own score. Only abstract-level numbers extracted; no per-dataset breakdown.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a self-reported confidence works as a switch signal when compared within one question, not across questions.

source: Kopka (2026) Increasing LLM Accuracy for Care-Seeking Advice Using Prompts Reflecting Human Reasoning Strategies (JMIR)
finding: The only RPD vs rival-prompt comparison found. An RPD prompt (pattern match, then mental simulation) and a data-frame prompt (sense-making, no simulation loop) gave nearly the same overall gain, so the mental simulation step is not shown to add anything.
numbers: 13,500 assessments, 45 vignettes. Default 63.3% (CI 61.9-64.7); RPD 67.6% (66.3-69); data-frame 66.7% (65.3-68). RPD OR 2.26, data-frame OR 2.05. Self-care: 13.4% default, 29.8% RPD, 24.6% data-frame. Only 2 emergency vignettes; 88% of errors were over-triage.
limits: RPD vs data-frame is not an ablation of the simulation step. CIs overlap. Gain is mostly on 13 self-care vignettes. No equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partial: no clean ablation of RPD step 3 exists. The nearest comparison shows no reliable extra gain over a prompt without simulation.

source: Li et al. (2024) Chain of Code: Reasoning with a Language Model-Augmented Code Emulator (ICML 2024, arXiv 2312.04474)
finding: Letting the model simulate code lines it cannot run (an 'LMulator') while a real interpreter runs the rest beats plain thought chains. Real execution gives near 100% where the code is right.
numbers: BIG-Bench Hard, text-davinci-003: direct 55, CoT 72, CoC 84 (single task); PaLM 2-S: 49, 61, 78. Cross-task: 50, 55, 61. Python-only variant fails on non-algorithmic tasks.
limits: Mixes code execution with LM simulation; it is not the same as asking a model to imagine one chosen action. Ablations separate interpreter from LM simulation, not simulation vs naming the typical case.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: external execution beats imagined execution where available. Mental simulation is a fallback, not a check.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling (arXiv 2407.21787)
finding: With an automatic verifier, coverage (any sample solves it) grows roughly log-linearly over four orders of magnitude of samples. Without a verifier, majority vote and reward models plateau.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: DeepSeek-Coder-V2 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples, vs single-sample state of the art 43%.
limits: Fixed per-item sampling; not an adaptive fast-then-check design. The verifier is the key condition.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a verifier (code check) is what lets many cheap attempts beat one careful attempt. Where no verifier exists, extra attempts stop paying.

source: Mattingsdal (2026) Assessing Military Professionals' Endorsement of Decision-Making Assumptions: An Exploratory Factor Analysis (Behav Sci 16:604)
finding: A survey of Norwegian armed forces personnel tested whether people endorse Klein's 11 claims as one belief. They did not: two factors fit better (planning/structure and analytic/evidence), explaining 29.24% of variance.
numbers: N=225 active-duty personnel (2024-2025); 9 items kept after dropping two; KMO=0.741; Bartlett chi2(36)=282.86; alpha .65 and about .71.
limits: Measures beliefs about decision making, not actual decisions. Not a replication of the 80% finding. Listed so it is not mistaken for one.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: no independent count of recognition vs comparison decisions in military data was found; this is a belief survey.

source: Lavoie et al. (2024) Dimensional analysis of experienced ICU nurses' decision-making for bleeding after cardiac surgery (Nurs Crit Care 29:1119)
finding: ICU nurses were interviewed with the critical decision method under the RPD model. They recognised bleeding types (normal, medical, surgical, tamponade) and matched actions to them. No count of recognition vs comparison decisions is in the abstract.
numbers: 39 experienced nurses, four adult ICUs, semi-structured critical decision method interviews, dimensional analysis.
limits: Abstract only. Qualitative, with RPD as the starting frame, so not independent of RPD's own coding. No counts.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open: RPD-framed work in ICU gives themes, not the share of decisions that skip option comparison.
